abstract: We ask whether small, open-weight decision models can support vulnerability discovery in open-source software at scale and what the surrounding system must provide. These models answer a typed question in one forward pass, returning scores for the permitted answers rather than text. Our harness selects widely packaged C and C++ projects and uses deterministic incomplete-fix miners and shape localizers to decide where to look. Intern-Decision-4B, a 4B-parameter open-weight decision model, then scores every candidate function. The scores rank the queues rather than accept or reject candidates, apart from a low reach-score floor that some queues kept. The search uses no frontier model. Alone, the model is weak: it separates vulnerable from benign functions with AUC 0.73, but a vulnerable function from its own patch with only 0.56. It is more useful for ordering candidates. On 75 public CVEs from projects without any of our findings, the fixed function reached its repository's top 25 in 21% of cases, 1.4 times as often as under random order of the same queues. Recall is bounded mainly by where the localizers look. On the campaign's own queues the model's order placed 7.5 times more confirmed findings in the top 10 than random order, an observed, selection-biased upper bound. On three GB10 systems, the harness searched more than 4,000 projects at 900-1,100 repositories per hour. The campaign confirmed 187 memory-safety findings; by worst-case CVSS v3.1, 12 are critical, 148 high, 23 medium and 4 low. The decision step runs at 4.4 decisions per second on one GB10 and 9.8 on a consumer RTX 4090 gaming PC, with matching scores. A small decision model supports vulnerability discovery through prioritization, while deterministic analysis and verification remain essential. All confirmed findings are being disclosed to maintainers under coordinated disclosure before publication.

title: Look Here, Then Decide: Small Decision Models in a Harness Find Memory-Safety Vulnerabilities at Scale on Commodity GPUs
